paragraphs.text: Yoma 62a — “The two goats of Yom Kippur should ideally be alike in appearance, height and value, and should be bought together. Even if they are not alike, they are valid; if one was bought today and the other tomorrow, they are valid.” Their initial equivalence makes the lot’s designation conspicuous: their two different ritual destinies are not determined by an outward distinction between them.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Rabbi Shneur Zalman of Liadi, Torah Ohr, Hosafos, Megillas Esther, “Al ken kar’u,” §3; digital 4:6 — “Haman therefore cast the lot, for a lot belongs to a level above understanding. Through understanding one chooses according to a reason and an intellectual consideration, with the ability to select. With a lot, however, one sets aside choice based on understanding and makes the matter depend solely upon how the lot falls, even against one’s understanding and choice. One therefore necessarily makes it depend upon a level above understanding: the will above understanding. This is also the meaning of the sacred lots: ‘Aharon shall place lots upon the two goats.’ As the lot falls, so it shall be; this too is the will above understanding. Thus, ‘He shall stand the two goats before Hashem’—specifically before Hashem, where sins do not separate and deliberate sins become merits.”

paragraphs.text: Connection: Torah Ohr makes explicit the inference underlying Rav Tzadok’s contrast between prophecy and a lot: prophecy enters the prophet’s understanding, whereas submitting to a lot sets aside the selector’s reasoning and preference. Its application to the Yom Kippur goats explains why their outward equality calls for a designation from a higher will. The act of accepting a decision beyond one’s own reasoning gives concrete content to the higher will identified here.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Tzidkat HaTzadik 40:1 — “The essence of repentance is that God illuminates a person’s eyes until deliberate sins become merits: he recognizes and understands that everything through which he sinned was also within the blessed God’s will.... Both divine knowledge and human choice are true, each in its own place: in the place of choice there is no place for knowledge, and in the place of knowledge there is truly no place for choice. When he attains this immense light, all his deliberate sins return, never having left the depth of God’s knowledge.... This is the mystery of the goat sent to Azazel: if a person did it on his own, he would be an outright idolater; but because the goat is sent by God’s will, which commands that it be sent, it becomes a commandment rather than a transgression.”

paragraphs.text: Connection: This passage explains both elements brought together in the maamar: the Yom Kippur goat and the retrospective transformation attained through repentance. It explicitly preserves human choice in its own domain; recognition of the deeper divine will is an illumination reached through repentance, rather than an instruction to choose sin.

Rav Tzadok therefore prefers the Mishnah’s sacred setting when explaining Joshua’s lot.

That proposal is his textual correction, rather than the wording of the retrieved Yalkut.

paragraphs.text: Sukkah 32b — “Rav Yehudah said: [A myrtle is valid] if three leaves grow together from one base. Rav Kahana said: Even two opposite each other, with one rising above them. Rav Acha son of Rava would seek out two opposite each other with one rising above them, since this had issued from Rav Kahana’s mouth.” The following opinion rejects that configuration as an inferior myrtle. Rav Tzadok’s analogy concerns the positive significance of seeking a form praised by a teacher, rather than resolving that dispute here.

paragraphs.text: Pesachim 120a — “Just as the seventh day is optional, so the six days are optional. Might the first night also be optional? Scripture says, ‘Together with unleavened bread and bitter herbs they shall eat it.’ ... Scripture says, ‘In the evening you shall eat unleavened bread’: the verse established it as an obligation.” The source distinguishes an obligatory first night from the remaining days. Rav Tzadok proposes that “optional,” relative to that obligation, still leaves a positive value in eating matzah throughout the festival.

paragraphs.text: Megillah 10b — “‘A cypress shall rise’—this is Mordechai, who is called the chief of all spices, as it says, ‘And you, take choice spices, flowing myrrh’; its translation is mira dakhya.”
